title: UTF-8, a transformation format of ISO 10646
summary: Specifies UTF-8, an encoding of the ISO 10646 / Unicode character set that preserves the US-ASCII range and works well with file systems, parsers and software that expect ASCII. It was designed for compatibility with applications not built for wider characters. It obsoletes RFC 2279 and is an Internet Standard.

eli5.summary: Letters from every language need to be saved as bytes. This clever code writes plain English letters the old simple way and uses longer codes only for other symbols, so old programs still work.

questions: what is the utf-8 byte order mark
why are overlong utf-8 sequences dangerous
subtitle: How every Unicode character becomes one to four bytes, with plain ASCII left exactly as it was.

tldr.problem: The standard encodings of the Universal Character Set used units larger than one octet, which made them hard to use in applications and protocols that assume 7 or 8 bit characters.
tldr.mechanism: UTF-8 writes each character number as a sequence of 1 to 4 octets, where the first octet tells how long the sequence is. US-ASCII characters keep their normal one-octet values.
tldr.outcome: An Internet Standard that obsoletes RFC 2279. Software must reject invalid sequences, because decoding them can be a security hole.

today: RFC 3629 is an Internet Standard (STD 63) and the text lists no later RFC that obsoletes it. It obsoletes RFC 2279.

sections.title: Why UTF-8 Exists
sections.content:
ISO/IEC 10646 defines the Universal Character Set (UCS), which covers most of the world's writing systems. The Unicode standard defines the same set of characters. Both define several encoding forms: UTF-8, UCS-2, UTF-16, UCS-4 and UTF-32.

All of them except UTF-8 use an encoding unit larger than one octet. That makes them hard to use in applications and protocols that assume 8 or even 7 bit characters. UTF-8 has a one-octet encoding unit and keeps the full US-ASCII range: an ASCII character is one octet with its normal ASCII value, and an octet with such a value can only mean that ASCII character.

The RFC lists further properties. The first octet of a multi-octet sequence says how many octets follow. The octet values C0, C1 and F5 to FF never appear. Character boundaries are easy to find from anywhere in a stream, and sorting UTF-8 strings byte by byte gives the same order as sorting by character number.

UTF-8 was devised in September 1992 by Ken Thompson, guided by criteria from Rob Pike, for use in the Plan9 operating system.
sections.eli5: Imagine a code book for every symbol in the world. UTF-8 is a way to write those symbols down so that plain old English letters look exactly the same as they always did.

sections.title: How Characters Become Bytes
sections.content:
UTF-8 encodes characters in the range U+0000 to U+10FFFF using sequences of 1 to 4 octets. A single-octet sequence starts with a 0 bit and carries 7 bits of the character number. In a sequence of n octets (n greater than 1), the first octet starts with n bits set to 1 followed by a 0 bit. Every following octet starts with the bits 10 and carries 6 bits of the character number.

To encode, pick the row of the table that fits the character number, prepare the high bits of each octet, then fill the x bits from the character number, starting with its lowest bit in the last octet. The rows are mutually exclusive, so there is only one valid way to encode a character.

Character numbers from U+D800 to U+DFFF are reserved for UTF-16 surrogate pairs and must not be encoded. When converting from UTF-16, first decode to character numbers and then encode those. This differs from CESU-8, which encodes the 16-bit UTF-16 values and is not meant for use on the Internet.

Decoders MUST protect against decoding invalid sequences. For example, a naive decoder might turn the overlong sequence C0 80 into U+0000.
sections.eli5: Short symbols get short codes and rare symbols get longer ones. The first byte of a code says how many bytes belong together, like a sign saying 'three seats in this row'.

sections.title: The ABNF Syntax of UTF-8
sections.content:
For implementors who use ABNF, the RFC gives a grammar for valid UTF-8. An octet sequence is valid only if it matches it. The grammar spells out the ranges the encoding rules imply: for instance, a two-octet character starts with a byte from C2 to DF, and every continuation byte (UTF8-tail) is in the range 80 to BF.

The grammar also excludes the overlong forms and the surrogate range. The RFC adds a note: the authoritative definition of UTF-8 is in the Unicode standard, and the grammar is only believed to describe the same thing. Implementors are urged to rely on the authoritative source.
sections.eli5: This is a strict checklist of which byte patterns are allowed. Anything that does not match the checklist is not real UTF-8.

sections.title: Worked Examples
sections.content:
The RFC encodes four sequences by hand. The characters U+0041 U+2262 U+0391 U+002E (an A, a not-identical-to sign, a Greek alpha and a full stop) become 41 E2 89 A2 CE 91 2E. The Korean word U+D55C U+AD6D U+C5B4 becomes ED 95 9C EA B5 AD EC 96 B4. The Japanese word U+65E5 U+672C U+8A9E becomes E6 97 A5 E6 9C AC E8 AA 9E.

The character U+233B4, prepended with a byte order mark, becomes EF BB BF F0 A3 8E B4. The first three octets are the BOM and the last four are the character itself.
sections.eli5: Plain letters take one byte, many other letters take three, and rare ones take four. The examples show real words turned into bytes.

sections.title: The Byte Order Mark
sections.content:
The character U+FEFF is a real "ZERO WIDTH NO-BREAK SPACE", but it is also informally called the byte order mark (BOM) because it can be placed at the start of a stream as a signature. In UTF-8 the single-octet encoding unit makes the byte order function useless, and the BOM always appears as the octets EF BB BF.

U+FEFF anywhere other than the start of a stream MUST be treated as a zero-width no-break space, not a signature. Stripping an initial signature is RECOMMENDED only when really necessary, since it can upset things like a digital signature or a character count.

Protocols get advice by case. A protocol SHOULD forbid the signature for elements that are always UTF-8, and for elements that carry their own encoding label and can be expected to use it properly. It SHOULD NOT forbid it where there is no encoding label or a ban could not be enforced, such as MIME entities obtained from file systems, FTP or HTTP.
sections.eli5: Sometimes a file begins with an invisible stamp that says 'this is text'. UTF-8 files do not really need it, but some have it, so programs should be ready to see it.

sections.title: MIME Charset and IANA
sections.content:
The memo is the basis for registering the MIME charset parameter value UTF-8. It labels text from the ISO/IEC 10646 repertoire, including amendments at least up to amendment 5 of the 1993 edition, and is suitable for the text top-level MIME type.

The label deliberately carries no version number. A version label would risk an older application failing to recognize a newer label, when a generic label lets it process the data mostly correctly. The one incompatible change, the 1996 move and expansion of the Korean Hangul block (nicknamed the "Korean mess"), is judged harmless because there was no significant data using the old layout. The IANA charset entry for UTF-8 was updated to point to this memo.
sections.eli5: The name tag 'UTF-8' has no version number on purpose, so older programs still recognize it when the list of symbols grows.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The main risk is how software handles illegal sequences. A parser that checks the UTF-8 form of its input but still interprets some illegal sequences as characters can be fooled. One example: a parser bans NUL as 00 but accepts the illegal C0 80 as NUL. Another: it bans 2F 2E 2E 2F ("/../") but accepts 2F C0 AE 2E 2F. The RFC says this last trick was used in a widespread virus attacking Web servers in 2001.

A second risk is buffer overflow when encoding. The ISO description allows character numbers up to U+7FFFFFFF, with sequences of up to 6 bytes, so the range must be limited to U+10FFFF or buffers must allow for 5- and 6-byte sequences.

Third, the same visible text can be several distinct character sequences, such as U+00E9 versus U+0065 U+0301. That can matter in string matching, for example an identifier in a credential versus an access control list. The RFC points to Unicode Normalization Forms as the remedy.
sections.eli5: If a guard only checks the front door but a sneaky shape of bytes slips through a side door, trouble follows. Programs must refuse byte patterns that are not valid.

sections.title: Changes from RFC 2279
sections.content:
This memo obsoletes RFC 2279. It restricts the character range to 0000 to 10FFFF, the range reachable with UTF-16, and makes Unicode the normative source of the UTF-8 definition while ISO/IEC 10646 stays the reference for characters. Terminology was straightened out, and UCS-2 and UCS-4 almost disappeared from the text.

The warning against decoding invalid sequences became a normative MUST NOT. New material includes the BOM section, the ABNF syntax and an expanded security section covering Unicode normalization. The suggested UNICODE-1-1-UTF-8 MIME charset registration was removed.
sections.eli5: This is the second edition. It tightens the rules, adds a grammar and makes the safety warnings into firm requirements.
